concepts.label: Biodiversity and Our Dependence on It
concepts.cardText: India is one of the world's richest countries in biological diversity. We share this planet with millions of living beings, from micro-organisms and bacteria to banyan trees, elephants and blue whales. Biodiversity is immensely rich in wildlife and cultivated species, diverse in form and function but closely integrated through a multiple network of interdependencies. Humans and all living organisms form a complex web of ecological system in which we are only a part, and we depend on it for our existence: plants, animals and micro-organisms re-create the air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that produces our food. Forests play a key role because they are the primary producers on which all other living beings depend. These resources are now under great stress, mainly due to insensitivity to our environment.

concepts.topicTitle: Conservation of forest and wildlife in India
concepts.label: Why Conserve Forests and Wildlife?
concepts.cardText: With the rapid decline in wildlife population and forestry, conservation has become essential. Conservation preserves the ecological diversity and our life support systems: water, air and soil. It also preserves the genetic diversity of plants and animals for better growth of species and breeding. For example, agriculture still depends on traditional crop varieties, and fisheries depend heavily on the maintenance of aquatic biodiversity.

concepts.topicTitle: Conservation of forest and wildlife in India
concepts.label: Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
concepts.cardText: In the 1960s and 1970s, conservationists demanded a national wildlife protection programme. The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act was implemented in 1972, with provisions for protecting habitats, and an all-India list of protected species was published. Its thrust was to protect the remaining population of endangered species by banning hunting, giving legal protection to their habitats and restricting trade in wildlife. Central and state governments then established national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, and the central government announced projects for gravely threatened animals such as the tiger, the one-horned rhinoceros, the Kashmir stag or hangul, three types of crocodiles and the Asiatic lion. Recently the Indian elephant, black buck (chinkara), great Indian bustard (godawan) and snow leopard have been given full or partial legal protection.

concepts.topicTitle: Conservation of forest and wildlife in India
concepts.label: Project Tiger
concepts.cardText: The tiger is a key wildlife species in the faunal web. In 1973 the authorities realised the tiger population had dwindled to 1,827 from an estimated 55,000 at the turn of the century. The major threats are poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey base species and growing human population. The trade in tiger skins and the use of their bones in traditional medicines left the tiger on the verge of extinction; because India and Nepal hold about two-thirds of the world's surviving tigers, they became prime targets for poaching. Project Tiger was launched in 1973, viewed not only as saving an endangered species but equally as a means of preserving biotypes of sizeable magnitude. Tiger reserves include Corbett (Uttarakhand), Sunderbans (West Bengal), Bandhavgarh (Madhya Pradesh), Sariska (Rajasthan), Manas (Assam) and Periyar (Kerala).

concepts.topicTitle: Conservation of forest and wildlife in India
concepts.label: Conserving Biodiversity, Not Just a Few Species
concepts.cardText: Conservation projects now focus on biodiversity rather than on a few of its components, with a more intensive search for different conservation measures. Even insects are finding a place in conservation planning: under the Wildlife Act notifications of 1980 and 1986, several hundred butterflies, moths, beetles and one dragonfly were added to the list of protected species. In 1991, for the first time, plants were also added to the list, starting with six species.

concepts.topicTitle: Types and distribution of forest and wildlife resources
concepts.label: Reserved, Protected and Unclassed Forests
concepts.cardText: In India, much of the forest and wildlife resources are owned or managed by the government through the Forest Department. They are classified into: (i) Reserved Forests: more than half of the total forest land; regarded as the most valuable for conservation of forest and wildlife resources. (ii) Protected Forests: almost one-third of the total forest area, protected from any further depletion. (iii) Unclassed Forests: other forests and wastelands belonging to both government and private individuals and communities. Reserved and protected forests are also called permanent forest estates, maintained for producing timber and other forest produce and for protective reasons.

concepts.topicTitle: Types and distribution of forest and wildlife resources
concepts.label: Distribution of Forest Types Across States
concepts.cardText: Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests, constituting 75 per cent of its total forest area. Jammu and Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Maharashtra have large percentages of reserved forests, whereas Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan have a bulk under protected forests. All North-eastern states and parts of Gujarat have a very high percentage of their forests as unclassed forests managed by local communities.

concepts.label: Community Efforts to Conserve Forests
concepts.cardText: Conservation strategies are not new in India; forests are home to traditional communities, and in some areas local communities struggle to conserve habitats alongside government officials, recognising that only this will secure their long-term livelihood. In Sariska Tiger Reserve, Rajasthan, villagers fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act. Five villages in Alwar district, Rajasthan, declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri', with their own rules that do not allow hunting. The Chipko movement in the Himalayas resisted deforestation and showed that community afforestation with indigenous species can be enormously successful. The Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is possible and economically viable.

concepts.label: Joint Forest Management
concepts.cardText: The joint forest management (JFM) programme is a good example of involving local communities in the management and restoration of degraded forests. It has existed formally since 1988, when Odisha passed the first resolution for joint forest management. JFM depends on local (village) institutions that undertake protection activities, mostly on degraded forest land managed by the forest department. In return, members of these communities are entitled to intermediary benefits like non-timber forest produce and a share in the timber harvested by 'successful protection'.

concepts.label: Sacred Groves and Traditional Beliefs
concepts.cardText: Nature worship is an age-old tribal belief based on the premise that all creations of nature have to be protected. Such beliefs have preserved several virgin forests in pristine form, called sacred groves (the forests of gods and goddesses); local people leave them untouched and ban any interference. The Mundas and the Santhal of Chota Nagpur worship mahua and kadamba trees, and tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship tamarind and mango trees during weddings; many consider peepal and banyan sacred. Macaques and langurs are fed around many temples, and around Bishnoi villages in Rajasthan, herds of blackbuck (chinkara), nilgai and peacocks are an integral part of the community and nobody harms them.

concepts.label: Involving Local Communities in Resource Management
concepts.cardText: The clear lesson from the dynamics of both environmental destruction and reconstruction in India is that local communities everywhere have to be involved in some kind of natural resource management. But there is still a long way to go before local communities are at the centre-stage in decision-making. We should accept only those economic or developmental activities that are people centric, environment-friendly and economically rewarding.
